newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-INTERVIEW-ANI sees more profit growth.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-INTERVIEW-ANI sees more profit growth.

text.p: Australian National Industries Ltd (ANI) should recover from its problems with its investment in troubled German water treatment firm Holter and grow earnings for the rest of 1997, managing director Peter Stancliffe said.

"I am looking forward to being able to report three consecutive halves of improvement. At this stage, I would say I am reasonably confident we will be able to achieve that," Stancliffe told Reuters in a telephone interview on Tuesday.
ANI earlier said its first half net profit rose to A$16.33 million from A$5.19 million a year earlier.
Stancliffe said ANI was cautiously optimistic about the level of Australian economic activity over the next six months.
He said the company's steel products distribution business, Steelmark, was usually at the front end of any uplift in the Australian economy.

"In the last six months, it is possible to detect an increase in the level of (Steelmark's) sales per day. We think we are starting to see the beginnings of a uplift in the level of general construction in the country," Stancliffe said.
ANI had two divisions which failed to record improvement in the first half, Comsteel and the mineral processing divison.
Stancliffe said Comsteel had a major capital expenditure programme late last year to introduce a new continuous caster.
"We've had difficulty with the commissioning of that and it required us to bring back on line the old horizontal caster in order to meet our customers needs," Stancliffe said.

As a result, ANI had lost some production it wouldn't be able to recoup but was now was back on line with its new caster and confident it could maintain budgeted production from now on, Stancliffe said.
The mineral processing business was slow in the first half, Stancliffe said, but had recently won a couple of projects and ANI was now confident of a better second half for this division.
ANI's large investment in the Holter group did not fit into the group's long term strategic plan, Stancliffe said.
"We can realise those funds and reinvest that money in our core businesses and typically get (EBIT) returns of up to 30 percent...that's a much better outcome for ANI," he said.
Stancliffe said he could not predict whether Holter's losses would narrow further in the second half because of the uncertain nature of the group's operations.

"We have a number of businesses that we have offered for sale. As they are disposed of, the losses will reduce. Similarly there will be points of time as we go forward that if we haven't been able to sell those businesses, we'll take the decision to wind some of those smaller businesses down," he said.
Stancliffe said the other unpredicatable area was the timing of the sale of Holter's profitable waste energy business, SHW Holter Wassertechnik (SHW).
"There will be ongoing losses (for Holter) in the period. We hope they will be reduced," he said.
Stancliffe said the current timetable for the sale of the Holter's SHW division had the sale completed before the end of June.

He said a couple of Holter's smaller businesses were expected to be sold or wound down within the next couple of months while the waste-to-energy business would probably not be sold until sometime in the 1997/98 financial year.
